A Norway maple, from Europe, marked invasive in Vermont. Snap a leaf stalk: its sap is milky. Its native counterpart, a sugar maple, is the next stop, 4 m away.
A sugar maple, native to Vermont, 4 m from the Norway maple. Snap a leaf stalk: its sap is clear.
A Scotch pine, from Europe and Asia. Count the needles in a bundle: two, short and twisted; its upper bark is orange. Its native counterpart, an eastern white pine, is the next stop, 29 m away.
An eastern white pine, native to Vermont, 29 m from the Scotch pine. Its needles come five to a bundle, long and soft.
A Norway spruce, from Europe. Its side branches hang like curtains, and its cones are long. Its native counterpart, a white spruce, is the next stop, 6 m away.
A white spruce, native to Vermont, 6 m from the Norway spruce. Its cones are short, and its crushed needles smell sharp.
A Lombardy poplar: a narrow column grown from cuttings of one male tree from Italy. Its native counterpart, a bigtooth aspen, is the next stop, 5 m away.
A bigtooth aspen, native to Vermont, 5 m from the Lombardy poplar, with big, coarse teeth on its leaves.
A young kousa dogwood, from East Asia. It blooms weeks after the native one, with pointed bracts. Its native counterpart, a flowering dogwood, is the next stop, 16 m away.
A young flowering dogwood, native to Vermont, 16 m from the kousa. Its bracts are notched at the tip.
A Colorado blue spruce, from the Rockies, with stiff, sharp, blue-gray needles. Its native counterpart, a white spruce, is the next stop, 5 m away.
A white spruce, native to Vermont, 5 m from the blue spruce: softer, green needles.
